newsitem.title: UK: Royal Shakespeare Co. broadens arts sponsorship.
newsitem.headline: Royal Shakespeare Co. broadens arts sponsorship.

text.p: The Royal Shakespeare Co., which bills itself as the world's largest theatre company, is expanding sponsorship of the arts into wider opportunities for corporate marketing.
Sponsorship, once a poor cousin to advertising, has become increasingly important to companies in recent years as they seek to raise brand awareness and develop closer relationships with consumers.
But while sponsorship of sports teams and events has become a high-priced, high-profile business, arts sponsorship has hovered in the wings.
The Royal Shakespeare Co.(RSC), however, is changing the scope of arts deals with sponsors, while insisting that the change is entirely compatible with the highbrow world of Shakespearean theatre.
"We've changed the way we deal with sponsorship over the last few years," Ian Rowley, its head of press and public relations, told Reuters in an interview.

Although the RSC, like other arts bodies, has had corporate sponsors for many years, those deals were narrowly focused, Robert Fleming, the company's sponsorship development manager, said at its London home at the Barbican Theatre.
Previously, in exchange for sponsorship, companies typically received advertising space in play programmes and free tickets to productions to entertain clients.
But from the 1980s there was much more of a directive from the government for companies to get more involved in the arts.

"Sponsorship grew at the RSC at a rate that was much faster than at other companies," Fleming said, because the RSC realised good deals were built on developing a relationship with the sponsor, not just accepting money.
This would include showing how overseas tours and individual productions could be incorporated into marketing campaigns, as well as the overall sponsorship of the theatre company.
Royal Insurance, the RSC's long-time insurer and now Royal Sun Alliance, became its first sponsor in 1984.
When the insurer decided it would no longer be the RSC's principal sponsor, drinks manufacturer and pub owner Allied Domecq stepped in.
"When Allied Domecq came in they were trying to get some reflected glory from the RSC," said Fleming.

Allied, whose brands include Teacher's whisky, Tia Maria liqueur, Courvoisier cognac and Cockburn port, originally signed a three-year sponsorship deal. It recently renewed the deal, this time agreeing to sponsor the RSC over five years for 5.5 million pounds ($9.1 million).
"What Allied has tried to do is identify specific theatres or productions (of the RSC) with particular traits or brands," said Rowley.

So Allied's Firkin pub group, for instance, is looking at more experimental productions that draw a younger audience similar to Firkin's clientele. Firkins this summer will hold theatre pub quizzes to build on that link.
The RSC also encourages sponsors to be more pro-active in supporting their deals. "It means promotions, it means advertising," said Fleming.
Citroen cars, part of France's PSA Peugeot Citroen , recently used its sponsorship of an RSC production of "Hamlet" to market its cars via a lobby display for a chance to win a Citroen.
The RSC, however, says the sponsorship deals do not cheapen its own image.
"Sponsors are not going to want their logo on Hamlet's costume," said Rowley.
